cues.text: Section nine: change management.
IT change management is the discipline of controlling modifications to systems, so that useful changes can happen without causing unnecessary disruption.
It is important to separate this from organisational change management.

Organisational change management is a different thing: it focuses on helping people adopt new ways of working, whereas IT change management is concerned with controlling the changes made to the systems themselves.
Next, the types of change.
Standard changes are routine and low-risk, and they are pre-authorised under defined procedures, so each one does not need to be individually debated.
Normal changes require assessment and appropriate approval before they proceed.
Emergency changes address urgent situations, and they are handled through expedited controls.
The key point is that an emergency change means faster control, not an absence of controls.
Now consider the workflow of a change.
It includes these stages, in order: request, classification, impact and risk assessment, approval, planning, testing, implementation, validation and review.
A change advisory board, or CAB, may advise on significant changes.
The approval authority should match the risk of the change, so higher-risk changes need higher levels of approval.

Throughout, you should record dependencies, communications, maintenance windows, rollback criteria and ownership, so that everyone knows what depends on what, who has been told, when the work will happen, when to back out, and who is responsible.
Let us look at an example.
Migrating a production database requires compatibility testing, backup verification, a rollback plan and monitoring.
A staged rollout reduces exposure, because only part of the system is affected at first.
If a health check fails, that failure can trigger a rollback.
Emergency security patching may require faster approval, but it still needs evidence and a post-change review.
Finally, human adoption matters.
To support it, communicate the reason for the change, involve users, train staff, provide support and measure adoption.
This is why a technically successful ERP deployment can still fail organisationally: if employees continue using spreadsheets, the new system has not actually delivered its intended change.
